title: The nine hearths raise Seonaid Chiar to the flame
summary: The nine hearths of Dùn ìseal raise Seonaid Chiar of the house of Muireach to the flame at six-and-twenty years old, the youngest Keeper chosen since Muireach Liath's own day. Her grandmother, a cutter of the galleries all her working life, warns her that a young Keeper who bends once in her first year is asked to bend again for the rest of her keeping.

title: Three teachers of Cnoc bhàn set an unlit lamp before the Hall's door
summary: Three old teachers of the stag's school at Cnoc bhàn climb the mountain road on foot and set an unlit lamp on the stones before Talla na Lasrach, asking only to be let back among the cutters already working the galleries, and swearing to ask nothing of the vein aloud if the Hall will stop asking whether they have any right to stand near it.

title: Seonaid Chiar's guild judgment at Cnoc leathan
summary: Hearing two carriers of Cnoc leathan's guild each accuse the other of taking a fee out of turn, Seonaid Chiar asks only which of them had first offered to give the disputed load back, and, hearing neither had, tells them the Hall's grant is a right to carry and not a right to quarrel. The two settle the matter themselves before they have gone a mile down the mountain road.

title: Ruairidh Glas stands once more before the stone cup
summary: In his nine hundred and ninth year, Ruairidh Glas, holder of the Red Share, asks unasked leave to climb Dùn ìseal on foot and stand again before the stone cup, though no lord of a share is required to outside the quarter days. He says nothing aloud that any living ear catches, and goes back down the same evening to Dùn dhearg.

title: Ruairidh Glas dies at Dùn dhearg
summary: Ruairidh Glas dies in his own bed at Dùn dhearg, having lived nine hundred and ten years and never once returned to Dùn thais since the morning he shed the first blood of the strife of the heirs there. He outlives every soul who stood beside him at the ford where his grandfather's line first took the Red Hill.

title: The Red Share passes without a summons to the Hall
summary: Ruairidh Glas's son takes up the Red Share at Dùn dhearg without any summons to the Hall, as the Peace of the Threshold requires none where an heir is named and undisputed. The season's rolls, careful to name every lesser lord, stay strangely thin about naming this one, a silence the Hall's clerk lays to the household's own quiet rather than to any failure of the pen.

title: The four dead of the high gallery are buried on the Hall's own ground
summary: The four cutters killed when the roof of the highest gallery falls at Dùn ìseal are carried up and buried on the Hall's own ground, the one ground on the island no feud has ever been let to follow a man. Seonaid Chiar sets the last stone over the last of them with her own hands, which no Keeper before her is remembered to have done.

title: The first oak props are cut for the galleries
summary: After a season's argument over how a gallery roof should ever be held against another such fall, Seonaid Chiar orders timber props of oak set in every gallery the Hall works, the first timber the Hall has ever spent on the mountain itself. The first oak is felled and cut within the season, so that no gallery stands unpropped by the following year's cutting.

title: Seonaid Chiar dies above the galleries she kept
summary: Seonaid Chiar dies in her own quarters above the galleries at Dùn ìseal, eighty-five years old, having held the flame the better part of six decades. The nine hearths that raised her young choose another after her without any dispute the rolls think worth setting down.

title: The school at Cnoc bhàn returns its unlit lamp
summary: On word of Seonaid Chiar's death, the school at Cnoc bhàn sends no delegation and no message of grief, only the same unlit lamp its three old teachers once set before her door, carried back up by cutters young enough to have known no other Keeper, and left again on the same stones, still unlit.

title: Cathair dhomhain's shrine holds the Law to the grain
summary: The new shrine at Cathair dhomhain keeps the Small-Burning Law to the very grain from its founding day, a strictness the town becomes known for beyond any other pride it holds. Lowland households speak of it for a lifetime, though the town itself remains a place carriers pass through on the way to somewhere else.
